quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer:
Likely yes for WCAG conformance: Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.3 requires text and images of text to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against their background (3:1 for large-scale text); incidental text, inactive UI components, and logotypes have no contrast requirement [3].  
At Level AAA Success Criterion 1.4.6 the required ratios are 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large-scale text, with the same exceptions [2].  
If the grey text is visual information required to identify a user interface component or its state, Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.11 requires that the component have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors (except inactive components) [1].  
If you haven’t specified a background color, white is assumed for evaluation, and failing to specify a background or text color is treated as a failure because contrast cannot be evaluated [4].

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 2.5.8: targets for pointer inputs must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, or Essential exceptions apply [4].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 2.5.5: targets for pointer inputs must be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, except when Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, or Essential exceptions apply [2].  
So if your buttons are smaller than 24×24 CSS pixels they fail SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) unless an exception applies (for example properly spaced undersized targets or an equivalent larger control), and if smaller than 44×44 they fail SC 2.5.5 (Level AAA) unless an applicable exception applies [4][3][2].

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer:
Level AA — SC 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum): large-scale (large) text must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. [2][5]

Level AAA — SC 1.4.6 (Contrast Enhanced): large-scale (large) text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. [1]

Level AA — SC 1.4.11 (Non‑text Contrast): icons and other user‑interface components (visual information required to identify components and states) must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors (Technique G207 addresses icons). [3][4]

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer:
1) 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) requires that text (and images of text) meet a minimum contrast with the background (i.e., a “minimum” contrast requirement). [4]

2) 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) is a stricter, “enhanced” contrast requirement (this success criterion is Level AAA). [3][4]

3) Both can fail for the same implementation mistakes (for example, insufficient contrast because of background images or specifying only foreground or background colors). [1][2][5]

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast): Disabled/inactive user interface components (e.g., a disabled button) are exempt from the non-text contrast requirement — they are not required to meet the contrast rule for controls that are not operable [1][3].  
For active controls, any visual information necessary to identify the control or its state must meet a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio with adjacent colors (Level AA, SC 1.4.11) [2][3].  
Note: other aspects can still apply — for example, contrast requirements for a control’s focus indicator or cases where a low‑contrast presentation is an author choice (and thus not “essential”) are not exempted by the inactive control rule [4].

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast) requires user interface components and parts of graphics required for understanding to have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against adjacent colors [1]. Logos are generally exempt from this contrast requirement (assumed to be dictated by corporate/brand identity), but the exemption does not apply when a logo functions as a user interface component (e.g., a link or interactive control) or when a low-contrast presentation is an author choice rather than essential to the brand [4]. As a best practice, authors should choose a sufficiently contrasting logo variant or provide an equivalent UI component that meets the 3:1 requirement when the logo serves a UI purpose [4].

quality.question: Which success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2?
quality.answer:
The new success criteria added in WCAG 2.2 are: [2]

- 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — AA [2]  
- 2.5.7 Dragging Movements — AA [2]  
- 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — AA [2]  
- 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) — AA [2]  
- 3.2.6 Consistent Help — A [2]  
- 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — A [2]  
- 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) — AAA [2]  
- 2.4.13 Focus Appearance — AAA [2]  
- 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) — AAA [2]

quality.question: Is 4.1.1 Parsing still required?
quality.answer:
No — Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and has been removed; it is no longer required. [1][4]

It originally aimed to ensure pages have complete start/end tags and proper nesting so assistive technologies could parse content, but assistive technology no longer needs to parse HTML and those issues are addressed by other criteria. [2][3][4]

Because the criterion was removed, there is no current conformance requirement or level for SC 4.1.1. [4]

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow) requires that vertical-scrolling content reflow without horizontal scrolling at a width of 320 CSS pixels [2]. 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels at 400% zoom [1][2].

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer:
Level A — Success Criterion 2.3.1 (Three Flashes or Below Threshold): web pages must not contain anything that flashes more than three times in any one second period, or the flash must be below the general flash and red flash thresholds [1][2].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 2.3.2 (Three Flashes): web pages must not contain anything that flashes more than three times in any one second period [4][3].

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication (Minimum)): 3.3.8 included exceptions that allow some CAPTCHAs (for example selecting images of objects), so a puzzle CAPTCHA might be permitted under AA when those exceptions apply [4][2].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 3.3.9 (Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)): a cognitive function test (such as solving a puzzle) must not be required for any authentication step unless an alternative authentication method that does not rely on a cognitive function test or a mechanism to assist completion is provided [1].  
Additionally, 3.3.9 removes the 3.3.8 exceptions and explicitly forbids required steps that display selections of images/videos/audio asking users to identify ones they provided or that contain a specific object (e.g., selecting all images with a car) [2].

quality.question: Quel est le contraste minimum pour le texte ?
quality.answer:
Niveau AA — SC 1.4.3 : la présentation visuelle du texte et des images de texte doit avoir un ratio de contraste d'au moins 4,5:1 [4][2]. Le texte de grande taille (au moins 18 points non gras ou 14 points gras) doit avoir un contraste d'au moins 3:1 [4][2][1].  

Niveau AAA — SC 1.4.6 : la présentation visuelle du texte et des images de texte doit avoir un ratio d'au moins 7:1 (4,5:1 pour le texte de grande taille) [3].  

Les exceptions — texte accessoire, pur décor, parties d'une image contenant un contenu visuel significatif, composant d'interface inactif, et logotypes — n'ont pas d'exigence de contraste [2][3][4].
